results.input: AI story games and AI image modes including AI Dungeon, NovelAI and related story products

output.failure_modes: Context windows force truncation, and summarization can omit or distort facts; AI Dungeon explicitly notes that summaries may need manual correction and that regenerating historical summaries after edits is limited by cost and context constraints.[1] Trigger systems can miss aliases, overfire on ambiguous words, or create cascading context bloat; NovelAI warns that large numbers of relatively inserted lore entries can slow context creation.[2] Image references improve identity but do not guarantee exact details, and stronger conditioning can increase cost, latency, incompatibility, or unpredictability.[4][5] Repeated retries can produce visual drift, token/GPU waste, queue frustration, and false confidence if the UI does not distinguish canon from an uncommitted draft.
output.methods:
1. **Layered narrative memory:** AI Dungeon separates rolling plot summarization from a retrievable Memory Bank; its system summarizes older action blocks, keeps a higher-level story summary, and retrieves relevant details with embeddings/vectors rather than sending the entire transcript every turn.[1]
2. **Keyword-activated world knowledge:** AI Dungeon Story Cards and NovelAI Lorebook entries store characters, places, objects, factions, and rules, then inject only entries whose trigger keys are active. NovelAI additionally supports regex, AND conditions, always-on entries, cascading activation, insertion order, token budgets, reserved tokens, and trimming rules.[2][3]
3. **Player-editable steering layers:** NovelAI exposes separate Memory and Author’s Note fields, with Author’s Note placed nearer the generation point, plus quick access to search and edit lore without leaving the story editor.[3] This is a useful UI distinction between durable canon and immediate scene direction.
4. **Branching and recovery controls:** NovelAI preserves undo/retry branches, counts dead ends, and offers trim, flatten, and reset-to-prompt operations; it also exports stories, scenarios, plaintext, and styled screenshots.[3] AI Dungeon’s memory documentation likewise describes manual summary editing and warns that historical edits may require manual summary correction.[1]
5. **Reference-conditioned character consistency:** Midjourney’s Character Reference and newer Omni Reference let users pin a reference image, reuse it across prompts, adjust reference weight, and combine it with style references. The documentation explicitly says references guide rather than exactly copy the source, and that fine details such as freckles or logos may drift.[4][5]
6. **Conversational image editing instead of blind regeneration:** OpenAI’s public image documentation distinguishes one-shot generation, image edits, and multi-turn Responses API image workflows; an implementation can carry an image forward and force generate versus edit actions, while controlling quality, size, format, and compression.[6]
7. **Cost-aware mode selection:** Treat images as an explicit beat-level or panel-level action, not an automatic every-turn side effect. Public examples show why: Midjourney states that Omni Reference uses 2x regular V7 GPU time and is incompatible with several faster modes.[5] A comic mode should therefore offer draft text/layout first, queued panel rendering, caching, and selective rerender of only changed panels.
output.player_effect: Players benefit when the system remembers what matters without making them hand-author an ever-growing prompt. Retrieval keyed to active entities makes a world feel responsive, while a visible, editable canon layer restores agency when summaries or generations are wrong. Image references, editable panels, and branch/retry controls make visual storytelling feel like collaboration: players can preserve a successful character or composition, revise a single mistake, and understand which changes are costly or merely provisional.
output.synapticgm_take: **Steal:** use a ledger-first architecture with immutable event/state records, a compact editable canon summary, entity cards with aliases and retrieval triggers, scene-specific directives, and a context viewer showing what was injected and why. Generate a storyboard, dialogue, shot list, and panel thumbnails before committing expensive art; render only on explicit beat approval, cache by canonical state plus prompt/version, and permit per-panel edit, retry, accept, reject, and rollback. Keep character sheets, wardrobe/prop/location anchors, palette, camera continuity, and prior accepted panels as structured references, not merely prose. **Never copy:** private prompts, licensed characters, distinctive copyrighted styles, or opaque vendor-specific prompt recipes. Do not let a model rewrite the authoritative ledger, silently convert a failed image into canon, hide cost/latency, or generate unlimited art every turn; if continuity conflicts, surface a repair choice and preserve the player’s ability to decide.
output.topic: AI story-game memory and continuity-safe comic image modes

results.input: AI comic/manga/story-to-comic generators and visual-story tools

output.failure_modes: Image models remain vulnerable to identity drift, prop/location mutation, unreadable or incorrect lettering, altered costumes, contradictory spatial staging, and accidental invention of events that were not in the story. Reference controls reduce but do not eliminate this risk; style and structure references constrain different dimensions, while high-strength references can reduce variation and low-strength references can weaken continuity. Generation is also asynchronous and resource-consuming: Firefly explicitly returns a job ID/status flow, while Anifusion and AI Comic Factory meter operations through credits or speed tiers. “Unlimited” generation claims, such as Storyboarder.ai’s no-credit iteration model, are unsuitable as a per-turn game default because they encourage latency spikes, cost opacity, retry loops, and visual noise. Failure UX should show a non-canonical preview, preserve the prior accepted frame, explain the violated constraint, and offer targeted repair or a text-only fallback—not silently rewrite canon. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]
output.methods:
1. **Script/story-to-panel pipeline:** Storyboarder.ai accepts scripts or ideas, produces scene breakdowns, shot lists, storyboard frames, animatics, and pitch-deck exports in one workflow; this suggests SynapticGM should separate narrative planning from image rendering rather than asking an image model to improvise the whole comic each turn. [1]
2. **Layout-first page authoring:** Anifusion makes the creator choose a page layout, describe panels, then perform final edits in a canvas editor; it also supports speech bubbles, vertical text, manga fonts, inpainting, pose control, and high-resolution exports. [2]
3. **Explicit panel controls and regeneration:** AI Comic Factory exposes style selection, multiple layouts, captions, prompt editing, redraw-from-scratch, single/double-page modes, and custom caption language/editing. [3]
4. **Reference-based identity locking:** AI Comic Factory advertises uploaded character references and consistency across frames; Storyboarder.ai extends the idea to characters, locations, and props across shots. These are product-level patterns for maintaining a cast bible, location bible, and prop bible. [1] [3]
5. **Separate visual constraints:** Adobe Firefly distinguishes style reference from structure reference. Its structure API uses a reference image plus a tunable strength value from 1–100, and returns an asynchronous job for generation, making the separation between composition constraints and stylistic constraints concrete and implementable. [4] [5]
6. **Direct composition/camera adjustment:** Storyboarder.ai offers 3D camera-angle control to orbit, pan, tilt, and zoom an existing frame without regenerating it. For comic mode, the analogous control is a deterministic panel/camera edit layer that changes framing while preserving ledger facts and character identity. [1]
7. **Credit- and quota-aware generation:** Anifusion prices AI actions through credits, with model/operation-dependent consumption and monthly allowances; AI Comic Factory likewise states that one image/panel consumes one credit and differentiates normal versus faster generation. [2] [3]
8. **Non-generative authoring as an adjacent pattern:** Pixton’s avatar-and-comic workflow requires no drawing and emphasizes student agency, literacy, comprehension, and real-time visibility. Its lesson is that visual storytelling can remain engaging when users compose from stable reusable assets instead of regenerating every image. [6]
output.player_effect: Players benefit when visual output is an immediate, editable confirmation of a meaningful story beat: layouts make pacing legible, captions and bubbles preserve readable dialogue, stable references make the party recognizable, and deterministic camera/panel edits give agency without forcing a full reroll. The strongest engagement pattern is therefore **co-authorship with bounded choices**—the player decides what happened and can approve or revise a visual beat—rather than passively waiting for an opaque slideshow. Pixton’s reported educator outcomes around engagement, agency, writing, and comprehension support the broader value of letting users actively construct visual scenes. [6]
output.synapticgm_take: **Steal:** layout-first pages; a persistent cast/location/prop reference system; explicit panel-level regenerate/edit; caption and bubble editing; camera/composition controls; async job status; credit-aware batching; and a clear distinction between accepted canon, provisional art, and discarded variants. Generate only at durable scene boundaries, on player request, or as a low-frequency recap, with cached approved assets reused across panels. **Never copy:** licensed characters, recognizable proprietary styles, private prompts, or product claims as if they guarantee consistency. Most importantly, never let an image model decide ledger facts, resolve rules, invent consequences, or become the source of truth. The ledger should author the scene specification; the renderer should illustrate it. Do not make every-turn unlimited generation the default—offer a text/thumbnail mode, queue and budget controls, and deterministic fallback panels when rendering is slow or fails.
output.topic: AI comic generation and continuity-safe visual storytelling

results.input: Visual novels, Ren'Py/RPG Maker presentation patterns, CG event models, sprites and backgrounds

output.failure_modes: The main failures are combinatorial asset explosion, cache misses, and visual discontinuity: pre-rendering every outfit/expression/background combination consumes disk, memory, and authoring time, while large or unpredicted images can stall frame rate or interaction. [1] [7] Layer systems can still produce invalid combinations unless groups, defaults, conditions, and anchors are constrained; conditional images may load unpredictably if state changes while displayed. [1] UI/render side effects can occur at repeated or predictive evaluation times, corrupting state if rendering is not pure. [2] Save/rollback can expose inconsistencies when unsaved aliases, changed image mappings, or incompatible versioned state are involved. [6] RPG Maker-style numeric picture IDs and ordered commands are deterministic but brittle if IDs, z-order, or erase operations drift. [5] For AI, unlimited every-turn generation adds cost, provider latency, queue variance, retries, moderation failures, and identity drift; a missing or bad image must degrade to a known canonical sprite/background, a text-only panel, or a clearly labeled “visual unavailable” state—not block adjudication or silently rewrite canon.
output.methods:
1. **Layered sprite composition:** Ren’Py’s `layeredimage` model decomposes a character into mutually constrained groups and selectable attributes—such as body, outfit, hairstyle, and face—rather than requiring a separately rendered asset for every combination. This reduces asset count and supports deterministic expression/outfit changes while preserving a character’s canonical silhouette and anchor points. [1]
2. **Scene graph plus UI separation:** Ren’Py distinguishes story images shown through scene/show/hide from interface screens such as dialogue, menus, save/load, backlog, and status overlays. Screens can be shown implicitly, automatically, as actions, or explicitly, and multiple screens can coexist. [2] SynapticGM should keep the ledger/state layer, comic canvas, dialogue, and player controls separate so a visual refresh cannot mutate world state.
3. **Reusable transition vocabulary:** Ren’Py provides named, parameterized transitions—dissolve, fade, move, wipe, slide, zoom, iris, shake—and supports interpolation of changed image positions. [3] These are cheap presentation operations over existing assets, making them a strong substitute for generating a new image every turn.
4. **Event-command sequencing:** RPG Maker MZ treats narrative presentation as ordered event commands: show text, show choices, and picture operations. Its message system supports a face image, speaker name, bounded text window, position, preview, variables, icons, pauses, and fast-forward; choices branch into explicit event paths. [4] Picture commands use stable numeric IDs, positions, scale, opacity/blend, movement duration, easing, tint, and erase, with up to 100 pictures concurrently. [5]
5. **CG/event-image model:** A full-screen or high-impact illustration can be an explicit scene asset invoked at a milestone, choice, reveal, or relationship beat, then registered in a gallery or recap rather than regenerated continuously. RPG Maker’s picture layer is suited to this because an image is shown, moved, tinted, and erased through explicit commands; the event sequence—not image generation—owns when it appears. [5]
6. **Rollback and save-state continuity:** Ren’Py rollback is conceptually a save at the start of each user-interacting statement. Its saved state includes the current statement, shown images/displayables, screens, screen variables, music, and changed game variables. [6] This suggests snapshotting both the narrative ledger and the exact visual manifest (asset IDs, transforms, z-order, expression, crop, and transition) at panel/beat boundaries.
7. **Predictive asset loading and cache budgeting:** Ren’Py documents predictive image caching because decoding a disk image can take long enough to hurt frame rate; it notes a default cache of up to eight screens and gives approximate memory rules of thumb. [7] For SynapticGM, preload only the next approved beat’s background, sprite variants, UI chrome, and optional CG; keep generated assets off the synchronous interaction path.
8. **Declarative, side-effect-free rendering:** Ren’Py warns that screens may run repeatedly, including during image prediction, and therefore should not cause externally visible side effects. [2] A SynapticGM renderer should be a pure function of ledger snapshot plus visual manifest; generation, inventory mutation, relationship changes, and canon updates must happen in the adjudication/ledger transaction, not in rendering callbacks.
output.player_effect: Players benefit when text, faces, locations, and choices provide a stable visual grammar: speaker identity is immediately legible, emotional changes are readable without prose overload, and scene transitions give pacing and emphasis. Explicit choices and rollback/save affordances preserve agency and reduce anxiety around branching. Layered sprites and deterministic picture transforms make the world feel responsive while retaining recognizable characters; milestone CGs feel valuable precisely because they are scarce, authored events rather than disposable per-turn output. These patterns also keep interaction latency predictable because most turns update existing assets and UI rather than waiting for image synthesis. [1] [2] [3] [4] [6]
output.synapticgm_take: **Steal:** ledger-first event sequencing; canonical character sheets with layered body/outfit/face assets; stable scene and picture IDs; explicit z-order, anchors, crops, transforms, and transition tokens; milestone-triggered CGs; preload/cache of approved next-beat assets; rollbackable snapshots containing both world state and visual manifest; and a pure renderer with text-first fallback. **Never copy:** licensed character art, named IP’s distinctive visual identity, proprietary prompts, or hidden implementation details. Do not make image generation the authoritative source of character state, do not regenerate a protagonist’s identity every turn, and do not promise unlimited bespoke panels. Generation should be an optional, budgeted, asynchronous enhancement requested only by an approved beat or player action; the ledger must commit first, and failures must preserve a playable textual/comic layout.

results.input: Webtoon and graphic-novel presentation patterns: scrolling, gutters, lettering and panel grammar

output.failure_modes: Long vertical layouts can become slow to load, expensive to generate, and difficult to audit; slicing, compression, and narrow mobile viewports can also produce blurry art, broken balloons, or action hidden at the fold [1] [2]. Overly large gutters feel like dead air, while uniform gutters flatten drama. Non-grid layouts, overlaps, and ambiguous focal points can cause readers to lose order [3]. AI image generation adds latency, token/compute cost, typography errors, identity drift, inconsistent props, and contradictory depictions of the same event; regenerating every turn compounds all of these and can silently fork canon. A failure UX should freeze the committed ledger state, show the last valid panel set, expose a text/transcript fallback, label missing or provisional art, and retry only the failed asset with the same prompt-independent scene specification and event ID.
output.methods:
1. Use a mobile-first vertical canvas with a single dominant downward reading path. WEBTOON’s public publishing notice says Canvas automatically optimizes and slices long uploads to a maximum image dimension of 800×1280 px [1], while Clip Studio’s public guide describes vertical scrolling, uninterrupted reading, smartphone previewing, and sequential image slices [2]. For SynapticGM, render a deterministic scene stream that can be paged or progressively revealed without changing the underlying event order.
2. Treat gutters as authored pacing, not empty padding. In vertical comics, larger spaces can create a pause, focus attention on dialogue, or signal a scene change [2]. Map gutter size to explicit ledger metadata such as beat boundary, time jump, danger reveal, or player-choice resolution; do not let a generative model choose spacing independently of the narrative state.
3. Compose panels around narrow-screen legibility: keep dialogue short, avoid essential action at the fold, use clear speaker-to-balloon proximity, and preview at the target viewport. Clip Studio specifically recommends checking the on-screen smartphone area and notes that simpler art and reduced text help preserve flow [2].
4. Preserve panel grammar through explicit reading-order IDs and conservative transitions. Research on comic navigation finds that readers use layout constraints and may be confused by blocked, staggered, overlapping, or non-grid arrangements rather than following a universal Z-path [3]. A SynapticGM renderer should therefore assign panel order, focal subject, camera intent, and transition type before artwork generation; experimental overlaps should be opt-in and annotated.
5. Use closure deliberately between panels. CVPR research describes comics as combining explicit information with omissions in the gutter, requiring readers to infer unseen action, and finds that neither image nor text alone is sufficient to follow the plot [4]. Encode the missing action as a ledger fact or permitted inference, then reveal only visuals that are consistent with it.
6. Separate lettering from image generation. Generate or place speech balloons, captions, sound effects, and UI text as editable vector/text layers with font, size, line-break, balloon-tail, and localization metadata. This prevents unreadable glyphs and allows accessibility features such as transcript view, text scaling, and reflow without regenerating art.
7. Use color and surrounding negative space as stateful visual signals rather than decorative randomness. The practical guide notes that color can express mood, time, and flashbacks, and that the area around panels need not be white [2]. Define a small, persistent palette for locations, temporal modes, faction cues, and status effects; validate any palette change against the scene ledger.
8. Make episode boundaries and loading states legible. Because long vertical episodes are uploaded and displayed as slices [1] [2], use stable beat-sized chunks, skeleton placeholders, cached previously committed panels, and a non-blocking “generating next beat” state. Never hide a committed outcome behind an indefinite spinner; offer text-only continuation or retry while preserving the same event ID.
9. Support alternate presentation modes without branching canon: vertical scroll for immersion, page/grid view for navigation, transcript/log view for accessibility, and a “recap since last checkpoint” view. All modes should read from the same immutable scene and ledger records, not independently summarize or regenerate the story.
output.player_effect: Vertical scrolling removes page-turn friction and lets distance, pauses, reveal timing, and color shifts become part of the player’s pacing experience [2]. Clear order and concise lettering reduce cognitive load, while authored gutters create anticipation and give players room to infer what happened. Closure is especially engaging because the player participates in connecting omitted action, but the inference remains satisfying only when the surrounding panels and text agree [3] [4].
output.synapticgm_take: Steal the vertical format’s controlled reveal, intentional whitespace, mobile preview discipline, concise lettering, palette-based mood/state cues, and multiple reading modes. Implement a two-layer system: an immutable ledger/scene graph decides actors, facts, order, transitions, and allowed inferences; a renderer turns those commitments into panels, balloons, and optional art. Cache and reuse approved character turnarounds, locations, props, palettes, and panel templates; generate at beat boundaries or explicit player requests, not every turn. Never copy WEBTOON’s or any creator’s licensed characters, assets, branding, private prompts, or distinctive series style. Never let a visual model invent canon, overwrite a committed outcome, reorder panels, place unreadable text, or use a dramatic gutter/transition that changes the meaning of the ledger.

results.input: Tabletop VTT portrait/token/scene-art systems and visual state representation

output.failure_modes: The main risks are state drift and visual overload: independently edited scene tokens can diverge from the canonical character, wildcard/random art can change identity unexpectedly, and too many status icons, bars, labels, or effects can obscure the portrait. [1] [3] Asset-heavy scenes also create storage, bandwidth, decoding, and GPU costs; Roll20 explicitly gates Dynamic Lighting to paid tiers, while Fantasy Grounds notes format/codec constraints for media. [3] [4] AI generation adds variable latency, per-image cost, queue failures, and continuity errors in faces, clothing, props, lighting, and geography. A failed render must therefore fall back to the last approved panel, a deterministic token-plus-overlay view, or a text-only event—not block the turn or silently commit unverified art.
output.methods:
1. **Separate canonical entities from scene instances.** Foundry distinguishes an Actor’s reusable Prototype Token from each independently editable Placed Token, while optionally linking resource data across scenes; this maps cleanly to a ledger-first model with a canonical character record plus scene-specific pose, visibility, damage, and location state. [1]
2. **Treat scenes as persistent, named containers rather than generated backdrops.** Foundry scenes hold background/foreground layers, grid geometry, initial camera position, permissions, walls, lights, notes, and tokens, and can be imported/exported or reused through compendia/JSON. [2] SynapticGM should version a scene asset and its state separately from any comic panel render.
3. **Use deterministic visual overlays for changing state.** VTTs represent disposition, rotation, elevation, opacity, tint, nameplates, health/status icons, vision, and light as editable token properties rather than requiring a new portrait every turn. [1] Roll20 similarly configures vision/light on tokens and uses barriers plus fog/exploration state to alter what players see. [3]
4. **Use typed layers and attachment relationships.** Owlbear Rodeo separates maps, props, mounts, characters, attachments, and notes into predictable layers; attachments can follow characters and represent status effects, equipment, or spell visuals. [6] This is a strong comic-mode pattern for placing a stable character portrait beneath deterministic wounds, speech/emotion badges, weapons, and effects.
5. **Build a searchable, reusable asset library.** Fantasy Grounds provides filters for Tokens, Portraits, and Images, keyword search, previews, folders, paging, and campaign-local assets; it recommends organized naming and compressed WEBP where suitable. [4] Owlbear similarly keeps maps outside scenes so the same map can be reused across encounters and campaigns. [7]
6. **Support batch placement and duplication instead of regeneration.** Owlbear lets players drag assets from a dock, duplicate a token, and auto-increment labels for repeated enemies. [5] A comic-mode equivalent is to instantiate a known character/prop template and vary only pose metadata, crop, tint, or overlay.
7. **Make visibility, lock state, and spoiler control explicit.** Owlbear supports GM-only hiding, locked maps, fog fill, and scene switching; Roll20’s Explorer Mode preserves explored areas in grayscale. [3] [6] SynapticGM should expose a clear “known / revealed / secret / discarded” state and never let an image-generation failure accidentally reveal hidden information.
output.player_effect: Players benefit when the visual surface is **stable, legible, and causally tied to play state**: a familiar token anchors identity, overlays communicate damage or conditions at a glance, scene switching provides spatial continuity, and fog/visibility rules create discovery without requiring the GM to redraw everything. Search, duplication, snapping, locking, and reusable scenes reduce cognitive and operational load, preserving attention for choices and fiction rather than asset administration. [1] [3] [5] [6]
output.synapticgm_take: **Steal:** canonical character IDs with scene-instance overrides; immutable approved portraits and reusable location plates; typed layers; deterministic status/effect overlays; fog and reveal states; asset search, locking, duplication, versioning, and explicit previews; cached renders keyed by ledger state. Generate art only at scene introductions, major reveals, or deliberate “panel beats,” with approval and rollback. **Never copy:** licensed characters, proprietary art packs, private prompts, or product-specific UI verbatim. Do not make every-turn unlimited generation the default, do not let an image model mutate the ledger, and do not treat generated pixels as authoritative state. The ledger should decide who is present, where they are, what they know, what changed, and which visual revision is approved; rendering is a cacheable projection with visible failure UX.
output.topic: VTT visual state and continuity systems

results.input: AI image consistency methods: reference images, IP-Adapter, seed/style control, visual identity and panel scripts

output.failure_modes: Reference conditioning is approximate: distinctive small marks, logos, clothing details, faces at unusual angles, hands, text, and multi-character interactions can drift; IP-Adapter notes center-cropping limitations for non-square references and a quality/diversity tradeoff as image-prompt scale changes [3]. ControlNet can preserve pose or layout while still producing identity, anatomy, or prop errors. Seeds are not reliable cross-session continuity controls [5]. Multiple references and high guidance can cause conflicts, prompt overfitting, or style/identity leakage. Latency and cost rise with reference encoding, structural preprocessing, high-resolution passes, inpainting, upscaling, and retries; batching too many panels increases queue time and makes failures harder to diagnose. The UX must surface uncertainty, version/model changes, partial failures, and stale cached assets, and must never silently commit a failed render to canon.
output.methods:
1. **Separate identity, style, structure, and scene controls.** Use a character/reference-image slot for recurring visual identity, a style-reference slot or locked style profile for palette/medium/lighting, and a panel-level text brief for action and setting. Midjourney explicitly distinguishes character references from style references: character references carry traits such as hair, clothing, and facial features, while style references carry overall visual “vibe” such as color, texture, and lighting [1] [2].
2. **Treat reference images as weighted guidance, not ground truth.** Expose a character/reference-strength control analogous to Midjourney’s `--cw` and a style-strength control analogous to `--sw`; provide a small set of approved reference images rather than an ever-growing prompt. Midjourney recommends detailed text alongside a character reference and warns that small details such as freckles or logos may not reproduce exactly [1].
3. **Use IP-Adapter-style conditioning for implementation.** IP-Adapter is a lightweight image-prompt adapter for pretrained text-to-image diffusion models; its public implementation reports 22M parameters and supports image variation, image-to-image, inpainting, multimodal prompts, face references, and combinations with ControlNet [3]. This maps well to a reusable character “identity card” plus a separate panel description.
4. **Use structural conditioning for panel blocking.** ControlNet adds spatial conditions such as edges, depth, segmentation, and human pose to a diffusion model [4]. In comic mode, generate or let the player edit a rough panel block—camera box, character positions, pose, gaze direction, and key props—then condition rendering on that block rather than asking text alone to solve composition.
5. **Use seeds for reproducible experiments, never as the continuity system.** Midjourney documents seeds as an initial noise starting point useful for testing prompt changes, but says seeds do not save a style, character, or appearance and may behave differently across sessions, model versions, or settings [5]. Store the seed in the ledger for audit/replay, while treating references, model/version, weights, prompt, pose map, and approved assets as the actual continuity state.
6. **Make the panel script explicit and versioned.** Represent each panel as structured fields—beats, participants, canonical identity IDs, emotional state, location/time, camera/framing, pose/layout constraints, dialogue/caption text, required props, negative constraints, and continuity links to prior panels. The player should approve a storyboard/contact sheet before expensive final renders; allow per-panel regenerate, inpaint, crop, or layout edit without silently rewriting neighboring panels.
7. **Use staged generation and human checkpoints.** A low-cost pass should produce thumbnails or a rough storyboard; only accepted panels receive high-resolution rendering, lettering, and upscaling. Public comic/storyboard research emphasizes panel-level descriptions, layout and character bounding boxes, and/or human-in-the-loop workflows rather than one opaque prompt-to-page call [6] [7].
8. **Provide inspectable provenance and a repair UX.** Each panel should expose “why this looks this way”: reference assets, weights, seed, model/version, structural map, prompt snapshot, generation status, and continuity warnings. If identity confidence or required-prop checks fail, show a flagged draft and offer targeted repairs—“restore jacket,” “match face to Panel 2,” “keep pose, change background”—instead of silently accepting a new canon.
9. **Control cost and latency through budgets.** Default to one thumbnail batch, cache reference embeddings and structural maps, reuse approved panels for variations, and require explicit confirmation for high-resolution rerenders or multi-panel batches. Treat generation as a turn-level budgeted action, not an unlimited every-turn response; report queue time, estimated cost/credits, and what will be regenerated before execution.
output.player_effect: Players benefit when the system makes continuity legible and editable: a stable character card and style profile reduce the cognitive burden of repeating descriptions, while panel scripts and thumbnails let them direct pacing and composition before waiting for final art. Structural controls preserve intentional staging, and targeted repair preserves a beloved panel instead of forcing a full-page reroll. The most important trust signal is that the ledger—not a model’s latest image—defines canon, with references, prompts, settings, approvals, and revisions visible enough for the player to understand and correct drift.
output.synapticgm_take: **Borrow:** first-class character/style/scene reference slots; explicit strength sliders; panel scripts with canonical entity IDs; storyboard-before-final workflow; ControlNet-like pose/layout guides; targeted inpaint/repair; cached embeddings; provenance, approval states, and per-panel version history; generation budgets with previews before costly renders. **Never copy:** private prompts, licensed character likenesses, or a product’s proprietary UI/text; do not promise pixel-perfect identity; do not use seeds as the sole continuity mechanism; do not let a generated image overwrite ledger facts; do not auto-reroll every turn or hide cost/latency; do not force the player to accept a whole page when one panel failed. SynapticGM should fail closed on continuity-critical fields, preserve the last approved canon, and label any speculative visual as non-canonical until approved.
